newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends touch weaker, market underpinned.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends touch weaker, market underpinned.

text.p: COMEX copper ended weaker following a week of strong gains but the market remained underpinned by supply factors and firm LME backwardation, traders said.
Copper ended slightly softer because buying was on a scale down basis and not of the aggressive type which pushed up tags in the past few sessions, John Tyree of FIMAT Futures said.

"People are saying let's have a little wait and see. When Thursday rolls round you have to think about whether you want to be long in an up market on the day before Friday when people are likely to take profits," Tyree said.

May COMEX settled 0.45 cent weaker at 112.35 cents per pound, traded 113.95 to 111.50 cents. July, which now has most open interest, was down 0.55 cent at 109.90 cents. Volume was estimated at 15,000 lots.
Despite Thursday's losses, May is still 5.55 cents up on the week.

The blister smelter shutdown at Kennecott Utah Copper, and restart of stalled labor talks Thursday at Phelps Dodge's Chino mine, along with the on-going strike at Chile's Escondida and possible walk-out at Quebrada Blanca mine, were all helping to underpin prices.
Escondida declined to comment on union leader statements that concentrate production had dried up.
LME stocks also continue to fall, down 2,350 tonnes to 146,750 tonnes Thursday.
COMEX stocks on Thursday rose 1,070 short tons to 51,251 short tons. More metal was expected to go into COMEX depots following LME cash premium ascendancy over spot COMEX.
LME cash ended Thursday at 116.50 cents a lb compared to spot April COMEX which settled at 113.95 cents.
But driving force behind the strong tags was the LME backwardation of $200/$210, a result of shorts being squeezed in the nearby London dates, traders said.
In announcing first quarter results Thursday, ASARCO's chief executive Richard de J Osborne said, "We believe that consumption will exceed supply throughout the rest of 1997 and in 1998."
ASARCO added that it will crank up its Hayden concentrator in Arizona to full capacity in May. Output at one of the two concentrators was cut from last October to reduce concentrate stockpiles.
